title: Boiled Ugandan Sweet Potatoes
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Peeled straight into cold water so they do not darken, then boiled in water that covers them only halfway — the top half finishes by steam.
longDesc: Ugandan sweet potatoes are white-fleshed, dry and starchy rather than the orange sweet kind, and they are the standard partner for malakwang, groundnut sauce and beans. Two details make the difference. The peeled potatoes go straight into cold water, which stops them discolouring while you work through the pile. And the cooking water covers them only halfway, so the bottom boils and the top steams — which keeps them from going waterlogged.
ingredients: Fresh Ugandan sweet potatoes — as many as you need
steps: Fill the saucepan halfway with cold water.
Peel the sweet potatoes and put them straight into the water as you go.
Scrape or cut out any dark spots and wash them thoroughly.
Cut them to whatever size you want.
Add hot or cold water to the pan so it covers the potatoes halfway — no more.
Cover the pan with the lid and boil for 25 minutes.
Test the softness by poking one or two with a skewer or the point of a knife.
chefTips: Peeled potatoes go straight into the water. Left on the board they darken within minutes, which does not affect the taste but looks wrong.
Water halfway up, not covering. The top half steams under the lid and the potatoes stay dry and floury rather than sodden.
Keep the lid on. Without it the steam escapes and the top never cooks.
No weight is given in the source — this is cooked to however many you need, which is how it works in practice.
Twenty-five minutes is the guide and the skewer is the measure.
These are the dry white-fleshed Ugandan variety. Orange sweet potatoes cook faster, go wetter and are a different thing on the plate.
Cut them large. Small pieces break up and absorb water.
commonMistakes: Leaving peeled potatoes out to darken.
Going by the clock rather than the skewer.
sources: Adapted from 'How To Boil Ugandan Sweet Potatoes', Amuna Foods (29 August 2021) — the peel-into-cold-water step, the halfway water level, the 25-minute covered boil and the skewer test are as printed there, with a stated yield of 6 servings and no weight given for the potatoes.

A second Amuna page, the Ugandan African Feast composite (12 September 2021), gives 1 kg of sweet potatoes boiled 20 to 25 minutes for 10 servings, which is the only weight the source provides anywhere.
reheating: Steam for a few minutes, or fry the leftovers in a little oil.
healthBenefits: High in fibre, potassium and vitamin C.
A slow-release carbohydrate with a lower glycaemic impact than white potato.
Boiled with nothing added at all.
The white-fleshed Ugandan varieties are starchier and less sugary than orange types.
culturalNote: Lumonde is the plain partner to Uganda's sauces, and it is what malakwang is served on in the north as a matter of course. It is also the most forgiving staple in the country — it grows in poor soil, keeps in the ground, and needs nothing but water and a pan.
